title: Sanjeev Kapoor Takes Indian Cuisine to MasterChef Australia, Challenges Contestants to Cook With Indian Flavors
excerpt: India's most recognized chef appeared as a guest judge on Season 18, bringing a mystery box of Indian ingredients and praising a contestant's creative take on dal and curry.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Sanjeev Kapoor guest judged MasterChef Australia, showcasing Indian ingredients in a mystery box challenge.
  • Contestant Casper Kenworthy won with a creative sweet potato and spinach curry dish.
  • Kapoor emphasized the need for Indian cuisine to evolve beyond butter chicken and biryani.
  • He praised the professionalism of MasterChef Australia compared to Indian cooking shows.
  • Kapoor advocates for highlighting home-cooked Indian dishes like khichdi on the global stage.

  • Sanjeev Kapoor appeared as guest judge on MasterChef Australia Season 18, challenging contestants with a mystery box filled entirely with Indian ingredients.
  • Contestant Casper Kenworthy won the challenge with a creative dish of sweet potato and spinach curry with pickled mussels and finger millet roti.
  • Kapoor praised the winning dish as "outstanding" and said "This is what India is" — after initially questioning whether it qualified as Indian food.
  • The chef said Indian cuisine needs to go beyond butter chicken and biryani, advocating for home-cooked staples like khichdi as the next frontier.

Sanjeev Kapoor, the chef who brought Indian cooking into millions of homes through Khana Khazana — one of Asia's longest-running culinary shows — recently traded his familiar studio for the set of MasterChef Australia. His guest appearance on Season 18 of the globally respected cooking competition delivered exactly what fans of Indian food have been waiting for: a serious, sustained spotlight on Indian flavors at the highest level of competitive cooking.

The Mystery Box Challenge

Kapoor brought an entirely Indian mystery box to the competition, filled with ingredients ranging from moong dal to Indian pickles. The contestants — most of whom had limited experience with Indian cooking techniques — were tasked with creating dishes that honored the ingredients' origins.

The results were ambitious and eclectic. Dishes ranged from moong dal sweet dosa with lassi ice cream to lamb rack with dal, and from spiced lamb cutlets with sweet potato and coconut puree to a choux bhaji — a French pastry technique applied to an Indian street food concept.

"It was a dish that crossed culinary borders freely, and Kapoor's reaction to it became the episode's defining moment.</p> <blockquote class="pull-quote"> <p>"You think this is Indian?"

The winning dish came from Casper Kenworthy, who assembled sweet potato and spinach curry with pickled mussels, pickled guava, finger millet roti, and a moong dal curry-leaf coconut podi masala. It was a dish that crossed culinary borders freely, and Kapoor's reaction to it became the episode's defining moment.

"You think this is Indian? You think you can do anything and call it Indian?"

— Sanjeev Kapoor, to contestant Casper Kenworthy

After a pause that had the room holding its breath, Kapoor broke into a grin: "This is what India is." He called the dish "outstanding" — and Kenworthy earned immunity from the next elimination along with a one-on-one session with Kapoor.

What MasterChef Australia Gets Right

In a subsequent interview with India Today, Kapoor drew a pointed contrast between MasterChef Australia and its Indian counterparts. "When I was on MasterChef Australia, even though it was just for one episode, I felt it was, above everything else, a food show," he said. "Food should never play second fiddle."

He was also struck by the production's professionalism: if filming was scheduled to begin and end at certain times, it happened exactly as planned. "This is not the kind of time management I usually get to see in television productions in India," he noted.

The chef traveled to Australia specifically for the single episode — a first for him — and described the experience as reinforcing his belief that Indian cuisine still has enormous ground to cover on the world stage.

Beyond Butter Chicken

Kapoor has long argued that Indian food's international reputation remains anchored to a handful of dishes: butter chicken, naan, biryani. His MasterChef appearance was partly an exercise in broadening that perception. The mystery box included ingredients designed to push contestants past the familiar — Indian pickles, finger millet flour, curry leaves — and toward the kind of home-cooked, regional dishes that define how most Indians actually eat.

Kapoor's Culinary Vision
›Advocates for home-cooked meals like khichdi.
›Calls for a broader representation of Indian cuisine.
›Critiques reliance on butter chicken and biryani.
›Believes Indian food can gain global recognition.

"It's the tenderness of home-cooked meals like khichdi that can truly make a mark," Kapoor told India Today, referencing the humble one-pot rice and lentil dish that is comfort food across India's class and regional lines. His own recipe — a tandoori salmon khichdi — represents the fusion he advocates: a globally accessible protein married to a dish that every Indian grew up eating.

Kapoor is the second Indian chef to appear on MasterChef Australia, joining a growing list of international food personalities who have brought non-Western culinary traditions to the show's global audience. The episode is available for streaming in India on JioHotstar.
